muscles.name: Protractor pectoralis / cucullaris
muscles.developmental: Branchiomeric. Derives from cranial paraxial/lateral plate mesoderm caudal to the last pharyngeal arch, not from somites — the defining muscle of the head–trunk boundary.

consensus.origin: Fascia over the occiput and anterior epaxial/axial musculature; in gnathostome fishes, the dorsal edge of the branchial region.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal margin of the pectoral girdle — scapula, suprascapula, or cleithrum.
consensus.action: Protracts and stabilises the pectoral girdle against the head and axial skeleton; in mammals, elevates and rotates the scapula.
consensus.innervation: Accessory nerve (CN XI) or its non-mammalian equivalent — caudal branchial branches of the vagus complex. Not spinal.

occurrences.name: Cucullaris
occurrences.origin: Epaxial fascia dorsal to the branchial arches.
occurrences.insertion: Epibranchial/pharyngobranchial elements and the dorsal scapular process of the pectoral girdle.
occurrences.action: Elevates the branchial arches and stabilises the girdle.

occurrences.name: Protractor pectoralis
occurrences.note: In Lepisosteus the cucullaris develops from the same cranial mesoderm population as the branchial constrictors, supporting a branchiomeric rather than somitic origin.

occurrences.name: Protractor pectoralis (cucullaris)
occurrences.origin: Dorsal fascia and the posterior surface of the skull.
occurrences.insertion: Anterior head onto the lateral surfaces of the procoracoid and scapula; posterior head onto the anterolateral border of the scapula.
occurrences.action: Draws the girdle anterodorsally.
occurrences.innervation: Accessory nerve equivalent; developmentally distinct from the levator scapulae, which is somitic.
occurrences.note: Sefton et al. (2016) show the cucullaris and the somitic levator scapulae are separable by developmental origin even where they are topographically adjacent — the strongest available test of this homology.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Two heads arising together and diverging posteriorly. The anterior head lands between the procoracohumeralis and the dorsalis scapulae, which is the topological fix on its identity.

occurrences.name: Protractor pectoralis
occurrences.origin: Occipital region and cervical fascia.
occurrences.insertion: Anterior margin of the scapula and suprascapula.

occurrences.name: Protractor pectoralis (episternocleidomastoideus, partim)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Alligator and Crocodylus, from Meers's descriptions. Meers's m. trapezius, this record's crocodylian occurrence. A thin sheet from the thoracodorsal fascia ventrolateral to the median row of dorsal scutes, inserting fleshily in Crocodylus acutus and by an aponeurotic sheet in other species along the cranial edge of the scapula dorsal to the acromion. Its origin can look continuous with that of latissimus dorsi but is always separable. Meers locates that insertion "dorsal to the acromion", but skeleton.json records the acromion as absent in crocodylians and the validator rejects the row — so the landmark is not asserted here. One of the two is wrong and the disagreement is worth resolving: either crocodylians have an acromion process this dataset denies them, or Meers is using the term loosely for the cranial scapular margin.

occurrences.name: Trapezius (+ sternocleidomastoideus)
occurrences.origin: Nuchal line, nuchal ligament, and spinous processes of the cervical and thoracic vertebrae.
occurrences.insertion: Spine of the scapula, acromion, and clavicle.
occurrences.action: Elevates, retracts and rotates the scapula.
occurrences.innervation: Accessory nerve (CN XI), with proprioceptive contribution from C3–C4.
occurrences.note: The mammalian trapezius and sternocleidomastoid are subdivisions of a single cucullaris field. Their retention of CN XI innervation, despite lying entirely within the neck and trunk, is the classic evidence that innervation tracks developmental origin rather than topographic position.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Trapezius, both bellies. Pars cervicalis from the cervical raphe between C3-4 and T1, pars thoracica from the thoracic raphe between T2 and T8, inserting on the distal two-thirds of the cranial margin of the scapular spine and often reaching the metacromion. Every origin is raphe or fascia, not bone — which is why a muscle this large leaves so little for a fossil to record.

homology.notes: Homology of the cucullaris across gnathostomes is supported by three independent lines: branchiomeric developmental origin, accessory/vagal innervation, and consistent topology between the occiput and the girdle. Sefton et al. (2016) resolved the long-standing question of whether the tetrapod cucullaris is head or trunk muscle in favour of head.
homology.teaching: The single best example of innervation as a homology criterion. A muscle that ends up in the shoulder still carries a cranial nerve.

muscles.name: Serratus anterior
muscles.developmental: Somitic (abaxial); derived from the ventrolateral lips of the cervical and anterior thoracic somites.

consensus.origin: Lateral surfaces of the anterior ribs and/or the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae, by a series of digitations.
consensus.insertion: Medial (costal) surface of the scapula, typically along and near its vertebral border.
consensus.action: Suspends the trunk from the girdle in a sling; protracts, retracts and rotates the scapula depending on which digitations contract.
consensus.innervation: Long thoracic nerve (ventral rami of the anterior spinal nerves entering the brachial plexus; C5–C7 in mammals).

occurrences.name: Serratus anterior
occurrences.note: Part of the 'serrati' sensu Howell (1937a).
occurrences.origin: Anterior ribs and transverse processes.
occurrences.insertion: Medial surface of the suprascapular cartilage and scapula.

occurrences.name: Serratus anterior
occurrences.note: Part of the 'serrati' sensu Howell (1935, 1937b).

occurrences.name: Serratus anterior
occurrences.note: Retained despite the carapace; the girdle sits inside the rib cage in turtles, so the sling geometry is unlike that of any other tetrapod.

occurrences.name: Serratus anterior
occurrences.note: = serratus ventralis sensu Kardong & Zalisko (1998), Kardong (2002).

occurrences.name: Serratus anterior
occurrences.note: = serratus ventralis sensu Meers (2003).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Originates from the ventrolateral ribs and inserts by tendon along the entire medio-posterior scapular margin — a broad, thin girdle extensor.

occurrences.name: Serratus ventralis
occurrences.origin: Ribs 1–8 and the cervical transverse processes by discrete slips.
occurrences.insertion: Medial face of the scapula along the vertebral border.
occurrences.action: Principal weight-bearing sling; in Tachyglossus it is very large, consistent with the forceful digging stroke.

occurrences.name: Serratus anterior (serratus ventralis)
occurrences.origin: Ribs 1–8/9.
occurrences.insertion: Medial scapular border, concentrated at the inferior angle.
occurrences.action: Protracts and upwardly rotates the scapula; holds the medial border against the thorax.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Serratus ventralis cervicis from the dorsal tubercles of the transverse processes of C3-C7 and the first two or three ribs; serratus ventralis thoracis from the ribs of T2-T3 to T6-T7. All fascicles converge onto the medial surface of the dorsal edge and caudal angle of the scapula, sharing fibres with the rhomboidei.

occurrences.name: Serratus anterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eudyptes pachyrhynchus, Schreiweis's type species. Serratus profundus, four flat fleshy fascicles from the last two cervical and first two thoracic ribs dorsal to the uncinate processes, inserting on about the caudal half of the costal scapula near the vertebral border. The small cranial fascicle is usually absent in Spheniscus and Megadyptes. A wing-propelled diver: the flipper is the most derived forelimb in Aves, and these rows are an observation of a penguin, not of birds. That is exactly what species-level scoring is for — the old model refused this source rather than let it stand for the clade.

homology.notes: Present in every limbed tetrapod examined; a stable row across all six columns of Abdala & Diogo's Table 1. Subdivision into cervical and thoracic parts is a mammalian elaboration, not a new muscle.

consensus.origin: Axial skeleton — occiput, nuchal ligament, or the neural spines of the anterior vertebrae.
consensus.insertion: Vertebral (dorsal) border of the scapula or suprascapula.
consensus.action: Retracts and elevates the scapula; holds the vertebral border against the trunk.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal scapular nerve in mammals (C4–C5).

occurrences.note: Howell (1937b) and Abdala & Diogo's own dissections find no rhomboid muscle in urodeles. Some authors' 'basiscapularis' in urodeles runs occiput-to-scapula and is innervated by ventral rami of spinal nerves 1–2, but Smith (1926) himself listed basiscapularis as a synonym of the levator scapulae, not of a rhomboideus.

occurrences.name: 'Rhomboideus'
occurrences.note: Confirmed by dissection in Rhinella and described by Escariz de Peverelli (1965) in Bufo arenarum.
Never described in turtles and not found in Abdala & Diogo's dissections. Loss would be unsurprising given the carapace rigidly links the axial skeleton to the girdle.
Never described in lepidosaurs and not found by dissection.

occurrences.name: 'Rhomboideus'
occurrences.note: Reported by Howell (1937b), Dilkes (2000), Meers (2003) and confirmed by dissection.

occurrences.name: 'Rhomboideus' (superficialis + profundus)
occurrences.note: Sullivan (1962, 1967) report both a rhomboideus superficialis and a rhomboideus profundus.

occurrences.name: Rhomboideus (capitis, cervicis, thoracis)
occurrences.origin: Nuchal line/ligament and thoracic neural spines.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Four bellies — cervicis, thoracis, capitis and profundus. Cervicis, the largest, runs from the raphe between T1 and the atlas or axis onto the craniomedial dorsal edge of the scapula including the dorsal angle. Scored at the level the rows can carry; the four bellies are in `parts`.

homology.notes: The name is quoted deliberately. Abdala & Diogo argue that on their phylogeny it is more parsimonious to treat the 'rhomboideus' as independently acquired in anurans, archosaurs and mammals (three steps) than as ancestral to Tetrapoda and lost in urodeles, turtles and lepidosaurs (four steps). The parsimony margin is one step, so the result is fragile — and it requires three independent origins of a muscle with the same origin, insertion, orientation and function. They flag the missing evidence explicitly: detailed dorsal pectoral muscle studies in more lepidosaurs and urodeles.
homology.openQuestion: Is the archosaur 'rhomboideus' homologous to the anuran and mammalian rhomboideus, or a convergent axio-scapular muscle? Innervation and development data for the anuran and crocodylian muscles would settle it.
homology.teaching: A worked example of parsimony being decisive by a single step, and of why authors quote a muscle name.

muscles.name: Levator scapulae
muscles.developmental: Somitic. In Ambystoma it derives mainly from somite 3 (Piekarski & Olsson 2007); Piatt (1938) implicated somites 2–4 together with the hypobranchial muscles.

consensus.origin: Cranium (often the cartilaginous operculum in urodeles) or the transverse process of the atlas and anterior cervical vertebrae.
consensus.insertion: Anterodorsal margin of the scapula/suprascapula.
consensus.action: Elevates and protracts the scapula.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the first and second spinal nerves; in Ambystoma also by the hypoglossal nerve.

occurrences.name: Levator scapulae
occurrences.origin: Cranium, often the cartilaginous operculum.
occurrences.action: Elevates the girdle; the opercular portion is part of the aquatic sound-reception pathway.
occurrences.innervation: First spinal nerve and hypoglossal nerve.
occurrences.note: Voluminous in urodeles and includes the columellaris and opercularis of Duellman & Trueb (1986) and Carroll (2007). Piekarski & Olsson (2007) showed its development and innervation differ from those of the protractor pectoralis, refuting the older claim that the urodele levator scapulae derives from the cucullaris.

occurrences.name: Levator scapulae superioris
occurrences.note: In anurans such as Rana the ancestral urodele muscle is fully differentiated into two separate muscles: the levator scapulae superioris and the opercularis. The name 'opercularis' should therefore be restricted to anurans.

occurrences.name: Levator scapulae
occurrences.origin: Mainly the transverse process of the atlas.

occurrences.name: Levator scapulae
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin with the neck muscles on the lateral cervical ribs; fleshy insertion running the anterior scapular border from its anterodistal tip to the glenohumeral joint.

occurrences.name: Levator scapulae (+ levator scapulae ventralis / omotransversarius)
occurrences.origin: Ventral tubercle of the atlantal wing (levator scapulae ventralis); cervical transverse processes.

occurrences.name: Levator scapulae (+ omotransversarius)
occurrences.origin: Transverse processes of C1–C4.
occurrences.insertion: Vertebral border of the scapula near the superior angle.
occurrences.innervation: C3–C4 ventral rami and the dorsal scapular nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Omotransversarius, from the caudomedial aspect of the ventral surface of the atlas onto the caudal region of the metacromion and onto the deltoideus pars scapularis. Scored on the acromion: the metacromion is a carnivoran process of it and has no element of its own here.

homology.notes: Distinguished from the protractor pectoralis/cucullaris by somitic rather than branchiomeric origin and by spinal rather than accessory innervation, despite adjacent topology. The urodele 'opercularis' is part of this muscle, not a separate one.
homology.teaching: Pair with the cucullaris. Two adjacent occiput-to-scapula muscles with different germ layers of origin and different nerves — topology alone cannot separate them, development and innervation can.

muscles.name: Opercularis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; a differentiated portion of the ancestral levator scapulae field.

consensus.origin: Suprascapular cartilage.
consensus.insertion: Operculum of the otic capsule (the cartilaginous plate in the fenestra ovalis).
consensus.action: Transmits substrate-borne vibration from the forelimb and girdle to the inner ear; also braces the girdle.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the anterior spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Opercularis
occurrences.note: Only in anurans is this a discrete muscle. Together with the levator scapulae superioris it accounts for the single urodele levator scapulae.
occurrences.attachmentNote: A pectoral girdle muscle inserting on the ear. Anuran-only, and only in anurans is it a discrete muscle.

occurrences.note: The structure called 'opercularis' in urodeles is topologically part of the levator scapulae, not an independent muscle (Hetherington & Tugaoen 1990). Walthall & Ashley-Ross (2006) disagree in practice, describing a discrete strap-like m. opercularis in Taricha running from the cartilaginous operculum of the otic capsule to the anterior edge of the suprascapula — and assigning it the opposite origin and insertion to the anuran record here. Presence is left at 'no' because a single dissection does not settle the homology argument, but the disagreement is the point: the same structure is a muscle or a part of one depending on which criterion is applied.

homology.notes: An anuran autapomorphy arising by subdivision of the levator scapulae. Functionally striking: it is a limb-girdle muscle that inserts on the ear.
homology.teaching: Terminology trap. 'Opercularis' in an amphibian paper means different things depending on whether the animal is a frog or a salamander.

consensus.origin: Sternum.
consensus.insertion: Coracoid.
consensus.action: Draws the coracoid toward the sternum, stabilising the girdle's ventral articulation.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the anterior brachial plexus; nerve to subclavius (C5–C6) in mammals.

occurrences.note: Howell (1937b) confirms it is not a distinct muscle in urodeles or anurans.

occurrences.name: Sternocoracoideus
occurrences.note: Often divided into superficial and deep heads in Iguana and Sphenodon (Holmes 1977; Dilkes 2000).
Fürbringer (1876), Walker (1973), Holmes (1977) and Dilkes (2000) hold that it is not present as an independent muscle in crocodylians or turtles.

occurrences.name: Sternocoracoideus
occurrences.note: Present according to Dilkes (2000).
occurrences.attachmentNote: The only muscle on the internal surface of the thoracic cavity. From the dorsal surface of the craniolateral sternum (processus craniolateralis) and the first rib, to a large depression on the dorsal surface of the coracoid base. Matsuoka & Hasegawa suggest it keeps the coracoid-sternum connection flexible.

occurrences.name: Sternocoracoideus
occurrences.note: Ornithorhynchus retains both a costocoracoideus and a sternocoracoideus (Howell 1937b), consistent with its retained coracoid.

occurrences.name: Subclavius
occurrences.origin: First rib and its costal cartilage.
occurrences.action: Depresses and stabilises the clavicle.
occurrences.note: Howell (1937b) argued the placental subclavius corresponds to the sternocoracoideus of other tetrapods, the coracoid having been lost and its attachment transferred to the clavicle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: As the subclavius. With the coracoid gone the insertion transfers to the clavicle — Howell's (1937b) basis for the homology.

homology.notes: The sternocoracoideus–subclavius correspondence follows Howell (1937b) and is reviewed in detail by Diogo et al. (2009a). Mivart (1869) instead suggested the subclavius was part of the amphibian procoracohumeralis; Romer (1924) rejected this, deriving teres minor and deltoideus clavicularis from procoracohumeralis instead. The distribution is patchy enough (present in lepidosaurs, birds, monotremes; absent or disputed in turtles, crocodylians, amphibians) that independent acquisition cannot be excluded.

consensus.origin: Anterior ribs.
consensus.insertion: Coracoid.
consensus.action: Draws the coracoid toward the ribs; girdle stabilisation.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the anterior brachial plexus.

occurrences.note: Walker (1973): not present as a distinct muscle in turtles.

occurrences.name: Costocoracoideus
occurrences.note: Frequently divided into pars superficialis and pars profunda.

occurrences.name: Costocoracoideus
occurrences.note: Usually divided into pars superficialis and pars profunda (Meers 2003).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Klinkhamer et al. separate a costocoracoideus profundus originating on the lateral margin of the first few ribs.

occurrences.note: Dilkes (2000): not present as an independent muscle in birds.

occurrences.name: Costoscapularis
occurrences.note: Howell (1937b) reports a 'costoscapularis' in placentals, the coracoid attachment having shifted to the scapula.

homology.notes: Restricted to lepidosaurs, crocodylians and monotremes among the taxa surveyed. The homologies of the reptilian costocoracoideus and sternocoracoideus with the mammalian subclavius are reviewed by Diogo et al. (2009a).

muscles.name: Pectoralis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral (flexor) muscle mass of the limb bud.

consensus.origin: Sternum, clavicle, interclavicle and adjacent ventral structures — a broad fan across the ventral midline.
consensus.insertion: Deltopectoral crest of the humerus.
consensus.action: Adducts and retracts the humerus; the principal propulsive muscle of the forelimb in sprawling gaits and the main downstroke muscle in flight.
consensus.innervation: Pectoral nerves — ventral (flexor) division of the brachial plexus.

occurrences.name: Ventral fin muscle mass (undivided)
occurrences.note: Chondrichthyans have an undivided ventral (adductor/depressor) fin mass; no discrete pectoralis is differentiated.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.note: One of the four muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct in tetrapodomorph fish with their highest confidence — deltoideus, pectoralis, the forearm flexors and the forearm extensors — because a correlate is identified in the fossil and the muscle is bracketed by lungfish, coelacanths and tetrapods.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. Andrews & Westoll (1970a) read the ventral cleithral ridge as the anterior extent of the pectoralis origin and the proximal, preaxial extreme of the ventral humeral ridge as its insertion. Molnar et al. accept the ridge but not the process: Callier et al. (2009), comparing Ichthyostega humeri across growth stages, place the pectoralis process in the MIDDLE of the ventral ridge, which makes the preaxial 'pectoralis processes' reported in Rhizodus, Strepsodus, Sauripterus and Sterropterygion part of a continuous ridge. The insertion is therefore scored on the undivided ridge — not on a process, and not on the deltopectoral crest, which is where an earlier note here put it.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.note: Tiktaalik roseae. Molnar et al. interpret it as lacking a pectoralis process: the ventral humeral ridge is confluent with the entepicondyle and undivided, and they place the separation of the pectoralis from the coracobrachialis one node crownward, at the last common ancestor of Tetrapoda, marked by a distinct pectoralis process and coracobrachialis fossa. So the pectoralis is not resolvable as a separate muscle here, and the row records that rather than a presence. The paired sulci on the internal and external margins of its coracoid foramen do mark a musculotendinous bundle running from the dorsomedial coracoid to the ventral humerus (Shubin et al. 2006), but no source names the muscle.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. The deltopectoral crest occupies the anterior portion of the ventral humerus (Coates 1996), the pectoral and deltoid processes united into one crest. Ichthyostega and the Catskill humerus differ: there the pectoralis process is separated from the deltoid process by the prepectoral space and is confluent with the ventral humeral ridge instead, which Callier et al. (2009) and Ahlberg (2011) read as the pectoralis still emerging from a larger ventral muscle mass. No origin is scored — few stem-tetrapod fossils preserve the ventral edge of the coracoid plate, so Molnar et al. could not trace the ventral girdle origins.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. A rugose, slightly recessed region on the posterior lateral wings of the interclavicle, read by Bishop (2014) as part of the pectoralis origin; one of the six muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct here with their highest confidence. They accept interclavicular scars for the superficial ventral muscles only tentatively, since the ventral coracoid plate that would carry the rest of the origin is rarely preserved. Striations distinct from the dermal ornamentation are reported on the interclavicle of Greererpeton too. No humeral insertion is itemised for this taxon.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.origin: Midline aponeurosis, sternum, and the tendinous inscriptions of the rectus abdominis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The insertion resolves to the crista ventralis — the salamander name for the deltopectoral crest — rather than to the proximal humerus generally. A refinement in resolution, not a shift.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.action: In anurans the pectoralis is a principal landing-force absorber rather than a propulsive muscle; its enlargement is part of the saltatory forelimb complex.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.note: = pectoralis major sensu Wyneken (2001).

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.origin: Sternum, interclavicle and the sternal ribs.
occurrences.innervation: Pectoral branches arising from the ventral divisions of the brachial plexus; in South American lizards the plexus is typically formed from spinal nerves 5–9 with considerable interspecific variation in root composition (Navarro et al. 2023).
occurrences.note: Present in all major extant reptilian clades (Fürbringer 1876; Walker 1973; Holmes 1977; Dilkes 2000).

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy along the ventral midline from interclavicle and sternal ribs; tendinous onto the deltopectoral crest.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.origin: Sternal keel (carina), furcula and sternocoracoclavicular membrane.
occurrences.action: Wing downstroke. The largest muscle in the body of most flying birds.
occurrences.note: Includes the pectoralis pars thoracica sensu Maxwell & Larsson (2007). The penguin pectoralis thoracica arises from the lateral sternal edge posterior to the coracobrachialis caudalis and from the trabecula lateralis, with a ribbon-like pars subcutanea abdominalis. Schreiweis (1982) records that the SUPRACORACOIDEUS is very well developed relative to the pectoralis in penguins — the reverse of the flying-bird proportion, and consistent with a wing that generates thrust on both strokes underwater rather than only on the downstroke.
occurrences.attachmentNote: In Cygnus the origin is in three overlapping layers — shallow clavicle, deep clavicle plus carina, and sternal plane plus rib cage — all fusing distally onto the crista pectoralis, the avian name for the deltopectoral crest. The rib attachment is indirect, onto the surface of underlying muscle. Both pectoralis muscles together are about 11% of body mass.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis (superficialis + profundus)
occurrences.origin: Sternum, interclavicle and clavicle — monotremes retain the reptilian ventral girdle elements, so the origin is more extensive than in therians.
occurrences.attachmentNote: More extensive origin than in therians because monotremes retain the interclavicle.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis major / pectoralis profundus
occurrences.origin: Sternum, clavicle, costal cartilages.
occurrences.insertion: Crest of the greater tubercle / deltopectoral crest.
occurrences.action: Adducts and medially rotates the humerus.

homology.notes: Present in every limbed tetrapod. One of the least ambiguous rows in the comparative tables — origin, insertion, innervation and ventral-mass derivation are all congruent.
homology.teaching: Use as the anchor when introducing the ventral/flexor mass. Everything else in the ventral mass can be located relative to it.

muscles.name: Supracoracoideus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass, but see homology note on the mammalian supraspinatus/infraspinatus.

consensus.origin: Lateral (external) surface of the coracoid and scapula, anterior/dorsal to the pectoralis origin.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus, on or near the deltopectoral crest and greater tubercle.
consensus.action: Protracts and abducts the humerus. In birds, uniquely, it is the upstroke muscle.
consensus.innervation: Supracoracoid nerve; suprascapular nerve (C5–C6) in mammals.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.note: Reconstructed from the homology hypotheses of Diogo et al. (2016) as much as from the correlate: Molnar et al. list it with the procoracohumeralis as reconstructable because similar muscles are present in extant lungfish, coelacanths and tetrapods.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. An ill-defined ridge between the proximal extent of the ventral humeral ridge and the deltoid-supinator ridge, read by Andrews & Westoll (1970a) as the supracoracoideus insertion. It is one of two correlates identified in this taxon and in no other tetrapodomorph fish, which Molnar et al. flag as reason for caution. No landmark is asserted: the ridge is not one of the named correlates they carry through the character mapping.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. The proximal ventral surface of the humerus divides into a smooth anterior region and a rough, concave posterior one, read as the insertions of the supracoracoideus and the coracobrachialis respectively (Coates 1996); the same configuration is described in Baphetes, Crassigyrinus, Ichthyostega, Greererpeton and Tulerpeton. Both muscles are scored as humerus/ventral, because the anterior-posterior distinction between them lies within that surface rather than being a second side, and which region each muscle took is kept here where it reads as the argument it is.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.note: Ossinodus pueri. One of the six muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct here with their highest confidence, on the strength of correlates Bishop (2014) identified; they do not itemise which scar carries it, so no attachment row is scored.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Ventral superficial surface of the coracoid cartilage.
occurrences.insertion: Crista ventralis of the humerus, adjacent to the pectoralis insertion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fan-shaped and parallel-fibred, its posterior part lying deep to the pectoralis and inserting beside it on the same crest. In salamanders the supracoracoideus is still a ventral adductor; the dorsal, wing-elevating role it takes in birds requires the triosseal canal, which does not exist here.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy origin on the proximo-lateral coracoid, covering the entire humeral head; fleshy insertion on the ventro-lateral humerus at the deltopectoral crest. Broad and triangular, forming much of the shoulder (Klinkhamer et al. 2017).

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Sternal keel, deep to the pectoralis.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal surface of the humerus, via a tendon that passes through the foramen triosseum.
occurrences.action: Wing upstroke. The tendon is redirected over the shoulder by the triosseal canal so that a ventrally placed muscle produces a dorsal pull — the pulley arrangement that permits both flight strokes to be powered from below the body's centre of mass.
occurrences.note: = pectoralis secundus sensu Jollie (1962). In penguins the supracoracoideus is very well developed relative to the pectoralis, which Schreiweis (1982) notes every anatomist working on the group has remarked on. In a flying bird the pectoralis dwarfs it; in a wing-propelled diver, where the upstroke is also a power stroke, the two approach parity. Same two muscles, same triosseal pulley, different force balance.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin restricted to the sternal keel and the tendon rerouted dorsally through the foramen triosseum, so a ventrally placed muscle produces the upstroke.

occurrences.name: Supraspinatus + infraspinatus (+ supracoracoideus remnant)
occurrences.note: Monotremes are the critical intermediate: the scapular spine is incipient and the supracoracoideus field is only partly divided into the therian supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The scapular spine is only incipient, so the supracoracoideus field is just beginning to divide into supraspinatus and infraspinatus. The readable intermediate.

occurrences.name: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus
occurrences.origin: Supraspinous and infraspinous fossae of the scapula, either side of the scapular spine.
occurrences.action: Supraspinatus abducts and stabilises; infraspinatus laterally rotates.
occurrences.note: The migration of this muscle from the coracoid to the lateral scapula, and its division by the newly evolved scapular spine, is one of the defining events of the synapsid pectoral transformation.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin has migrated off the coracoid — which no longer exists as a separate bone — onto the lateral scapula, where the new scapular spine splits it into supraspinatus and infraspinatus.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin restricted to the sternal keel and the tendon rerouted dorsally through the foramen triosseum, so a ventrally placed muscle produces the upstroke.

homology.notes: The supracoracoideus → supraspinatus + infraspinatus transformation is well supported by shared suprascapular innervation and by the monotreme intermediate condition. The avian supracoracoideus is homologous to the reptilian muscle; only its tendon path is novel.
homology.teaching: Two independent teaching payloads: (1) the synapsid coracoid-to-scapula migration, readable directly off the monotreme condition; (2) the avian triosseal pulley, where homology is preserved but mechanics are inverted. Third payload: compare the penguin. Schreiweis (1982) finds the supracoracoideus nearly matching the pectoralis in wing-propelled divers, against the large disparity in aerial fliers — a force-balance change with no change in homology, attachment or nerve.

muscles.name: Deltoideus scapularis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) muscle mass of the limb bud.
synonyms: dorsal or scapular part of deltoideus (Walker 1973; Wyneken 2001)

consensus.origin: Lateral surface of the scapula and suprascapula.
consensus.insertion: Deltopectoral crest of the humerus.
consensus.action: Abducts, protracts and laterally rotates the humerus; antagonist of the pectoralis.
consensus.innervation: Axillary nerve — dorsal (extensor) division of the brachial plexus (C5–C6).

occurrences.name: Deltoideus
occurrences.note: The deltoideus is one of the four muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct in tetrapodomorph fish with their highest confidence.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. Origin from the thickened posterior margin of the cleithrum just above the glenoid, which Andrews & Westoll (1970a) read as the deltoideus plus part of the latissimus dorsi — Molnar et al. label it 'del?' and note that a comparable posterior flange in Strepsodus and Megalichthys might as easily carry an undifferentiated superficial adductor. Insertion on the dorsal humerus with no landmark: the ectepicondyle, deltoid process and possible incipient latissimus dorsi process are close together and hard to distinguish here, and Molnar et al. hold that for muscle reconstruction it does not matter whether the deltoid and supinator processes are separate, since neither reading indicates separate muscles.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tiktaalik roseae. The ectepicondyle, deltoid process and latissimus dorsi process are clearly separate here, unlike in Eusthenopteron where the three are close together (Vorobyeva 1995; Shubin et al. 2006; Ahlberg 2011). The insertion is still scored on the dorsal humerus without a landmark: Molnar et al. put the deltoideus insertion on the dorsal ridge and its derivatives, and Boisvert (2009) reads the deltoid and supinator processes as a continuous flange in this taxon.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. Origin from a muscle scar on the lateral surface of the cleithrum just dorsal to the anteroventral process, where the cleithrum articulates with the clavicle (Coates 1996). Molnar et al. attribute cleithral and clavicular scars to 'the deltoideus and/or latissimus dorsi' without separating the two, so this row may carry a shared scar and the latissimus dorsi occurrence records no origin at all. Insertion on the deltopectoral crest, where the deltoid and pectoral processes are united.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. Longitudinally oriented, anastomosing ridges and grooves along the posterior margins of both the cleithrum and the clavicle, including the ascending process of the clavicle, read by Bishop (2014) as the deltoideus origin — two rows, because they are two bones. Comparable striations on the inner surface and ascending process of the clavicle in Crassigyrinus (Panchen 1985) and on the tip of the clavicular ascending process in Greererpeton (Godfrey 1989) suggest the same origin was general in stem tetrapods. One of the six highest-confidence reconstructions here.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.note: Corresponds to the dorsalis scapulae of Smith (1926), Howell (1937b), Romer (1944), Walthall & Ashley-Ross (2006).
occurrences.origin: Dorsolateral surface of the suprascapular cartilage.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The fibres pass around the anterior side of the humerus to reach a ventral crest — a dorsal girdle muscle with a ventral insertion, which is what lets it elevate the humerus.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Two heads: one muscular from the anterolateral suprascapula and scapula, a second from the ventral and inner border of the clavicle, both tendinous onto the deltopectoral crest. The suprascapular head is the one that disappears in mammals with the cartilage.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy on the distolateral scapula, tendinous on the dorsolateral humeral head.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.note: Part of the acromialis sensu Ribbing (1938); part of the deltoideus sensu Jollie (1962).

occurrences.name: Deltoideus, pars scapularis (spinous part)
occurrences.origin: Spine of the scapula.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Deltoideus pars scapularis, from the fascia over infraspinatus, the proximal scapular spine and the metacromion, by a broad flat tendinous fascia onto the middle of the deltoid crest just lateral to the acromial belly.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eudyptes pachyrhynchus, Schreiweis's type species. Deltoideus major, a very thin triangular muscle arising fleshy from the distal apex of the clavicle, the dorsal surface of the coracoscapular ligament and the acromial process of the scapula, converging on a short tendon that inserts on the caudodorsal humerus very close to the latissimus dorsi insertion. A wing-propelled diver: the flipper is the most derived forelimb in Aves, and these rows are an observation of a penguin, not of birds. That is exactly what species-level scoring is for — the old model refused this source rather than let it stand for the clade. Schreiweis names the **acromial process of the scapula** as the third origin; skeleton.json records the acromion as absent in Aves and the validator rejects it, so it is not asserted here. That is now the third source to describe an acromion in a taxon this dataset denies one — see the element's own note.

homology.notes: Present in all six of Abdala & Diogo's columns and in mammals. Together with the deltoideus clavicularis it forms the deltoid complex; the boundary between the two varies with the degree of girdle ossification.

muscles.name: Deltoideus clavicularis / procoracohumeralis
synonyms: ventral or clavicular part of deltoideus (Walker 1973; Wyneken 2001)

consensus.origin: Clavicle, procoracoid, or acromion.
consensus.insertion: Deltopectoral crest of the humerus, anterior to the deltoideus scapularis insertion.
consensus.action: Protracts and abducts the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Axillary nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.name: Procoracohumeralis
occurrences.note: Reconstructable in tetrapodomorph fish on homology grounds — similar muscles are present in extant lungfish, coelacanths and tetrapods — rather than from the correlate alone.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. A hollow just dorsal to the glenoid on the scapulocoracoid, read as the procoracohumeralis origin — Andrews & Westoll's (1970a) 'scapulohumeralis'. The nomenclature is the substance here. Molnar et al.'s procoracohumeralis has two homologues in Iguana, the scapulohumeralis anterior from the lateral scapula and the deltoideus clavicularis from the medial clavicle, so the fossil rows on this record are the undivided ancestral muscle, and the correlate's position above the glenoid corresponds to the scapular of those two rather than the clavicular. Molnar & Diogo (2021) reach the same place from the other end: reconstructions of the deltoid group across seven fossil taxa are nearly identical, and the scapulohumeralis-versus-procoracohumeralis dispute is nomenclatural rather than anatomical.

occurrences.name: Procoracohumeralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. Origin from the lateral fossa on the scapulocoracoid dorsal to the glenoid, observed by Molnar et al. on MGUH 1258 and 1300; the posterior fossa beside it carries the subcoracoscapularis. Their general reading of the stem-tetrapod girdle is that the two fossae, separated by the anterior glenoid buttress, mark two deep dorsal muscles with different lines of action. Insertion in the scapulohumeral depression of the dorsal humerus, proximal and anterior to the latissimus dorsi attachment — Coates's 'scapulohumeralis-like muscle'.

occurrences.name: Procoracohumeralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. Scarring over a large, shallow concavity on the lateral face of the scapulocoracoid, read by Bishop (2014) as the procoracohumeralis origin ('scapulohumeralis'), and one of the six highest-confidence reconstructions here. The same lateral fossa is identified in Hynerpeton, in captorhinids and in Pederpes, and Molnar et al. homologise it with the facet that carries the adductor profundus origin just dorsal to the glenoid in Neoceratodus and Latimeria — the fin muscle mass this one comes out of.

occurrences.name: Procoracohumeralis
occurrences.note: The amphibian name reflects the procoracoid origin; the muscle is the same field as the amniote deltoideus clavicularis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Called procoracohumeralis in amphibians purely because the origin sits on the procoracoid.
occurrences.origin: Procoracoid cartilage.
occurrences.insertion: Anterior surface of the proximal humerus.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus clavicularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylians have no clavicle, so despite the name the origin sits on the scapula — which is why Fürbringer (1876) called this muscle the scapularis inferior.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus clavicularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Nothoprocta pentlandii, from Widrig et al.'s contrast-enhanced CT atlas. M. deltoideus pars minor: fleshy origin on the lateral aspect of the acrocoracoid process of the coracoid and on the acromial process of the furcula, ventral and lateral to the origin of M. deltoideus pars propatagialis. Short-bellied, inserting on the proximodorsal margin of the humeral head. **The furcular head is the point of interest** — this record is the clavicular deltoid, and the avian furcula is the fused clavicles, so the homology is carried by a bone that no longer exists as a pair. Scored on the furcula without a landmark: the 'acromial process of the furcula' is not the scapular acromion, which skeleton.json correctly records as absent in birds — the validator rejected the row on both counts. Two different structures sharing a word.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus, pars acromialis and pars clavicularis
occurrences.origin: Acromion and lateral third of the clavicle.
occurrences.action: Abducts and flexes the humerus.
occurrences.note: Romer (1924) derived the mammalian teres minor and deltoideus clavicularis from the procoracohumeralis, against Mivart's (1869) suggestion that the subclavius came from this field.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The muscle is renamed at every step for the bone that happens to carry its origin, though the muscle itself is continuous across Tetrapoda.

homology.notes: Continuous across Tetrapoda; the name changes with the girdle element that carries the origin (procoracoid in amphibians, clavicle/acromion in amniotes), not with the muscle's identity.
homology.teaching: A clean example of a muscle renamed for its bony origin rather than for any change in the muscle itself — exactly the kind of synonymy the comparative tables exist to dissolve.

consensus.origin: Lateral surface of the scapula, anteroventral to the glenoid.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus near the greater tubercle.
consensus.action: Protracts and laterally rotates the humerus; stabilises the glenohumeral joint.
consensus.innervation: Axillary nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis anterior
occurrences.note: = scapulohumeralis cranialis sensu Dilkes (2000) and Maxwell & Larsson (2007).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Nothoprocta pentlandii, from Widrig et al.'s contrast-enhanced CT atlas. M. scapulohumeralis cranialis, a thin cord between scapula and humerus with a fleshy origin and insertion. It arises on the lateral surface of the scapular neck, cranial to the origin of the lateral head of M. subscapularis, and inserts on the proximal humerus at the distal edge of the pneumatic foramen. The scapular neck and the pneumatic foramen have no elements of their own here, so both ends are scored at bone level with the detail in this note.

occurrences.name: Teres minor
occurrences.origin: Lateral border of the scapula.
occurrences.action: Laterally rotates the humerus.
occurrences.note: Romer (1924) derived teres minor from the procoracohumeralis field rather than from scapulohumeralis anterior; the two hypotheses have not been decisively separated.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Teres minor, from the caudal margin of the scapula and sometimes by fascia from infraspinatus, by a thin tendon onto the lateral aspect of the base of the greater tuberosity just distal to the infraspinatus insertion. Absent on both sides of one of the six specimens, which is the kind of intraspecific absence `variable` exists for.

homology.notes: Patchy distribution (lepidosaurs and birds, absent in turtles, crocodylians and amphibians) makes the amniote-wide homology hypothesis weak. The correspondence with mammalian teres minor is proposed but unresolved — see the competing Romer (1924) derivation from procoracohumeralis.
homology.openQuestion: Is scapulohumeralis anterior a single retained muscle with multiple losses, or independently differentiated in lepidosaurs and birds?

consensus.origin: Lateral surface of the scapula posterodorsal to the glenoid.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus.
consensus.action: Retracts and laterally rotates the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Axillary nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.note: Abdala & Diogo mark this cell '– [but see text]' — absent in Timon lepidus but discussed as possibly present in other lepidosaurs.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis posterior
occurrences.note: = scapulohumeralis caudalis sensu Meers (2003).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin on the proximo-lateral and posterior scapula, insertion on the proximo-lateral humeral head, both fleshy. Klinkhamer et al. equate it with teres minor, which bears on the unresolved scapulohumeralis/teres minor question.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Nothoprocta pentlandii, from Widrig et al.'s contrast-enhanced CT atlas. M. scapulohumeralis caudalis, substantially larger than the cranialis. Its fleshy origin runs along the lateral scapula from the caudal margin of the cranialis origin to the caudal end of the bone; its thick insertion tendon passes ventral to the cranialis and spreads widely across the ventral margin of the proximal bicipital crest of the humerus.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eudyptes pachyrhynchus, Schreiweis's type species. Extensive origin from about the posterior two-thirds of the dorsal and lateral scapular surfaces; the fibres pass obliquely forward to a strong tendon inserting on the posterior border of the humerus at about a third of its length. Schreiweis notes it is a very uniform muscle across the Spheniscidae. A wing-propelled diver: the flipper is the most derived forelimb in Aves, and these rows are an observation of a penguin, not of birds. That is exactly what species-level scoring is for — the old model refused this source rather than let it stand for the clade.

homology.notes: An archosaur muscle on the sampling in Abdala & Diogo (2010). Widely used in archosaur fossil muscle reconstruction because it leaves a scar posterodorsal to the glenoid.

consensus.origin: Medial (internal) surface of the scapula and coracoid.
consensus.insertion: Lesser tubercle / medial process of the proximal humerus.
consensus.action: Adducts and medially rotates the humerus; a principal glenohumeral stabiliser.
consensus.innervation: Subscapular nerves (C5–C7).

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: Scored uncertain rather than inferred. Molnar et al. report that they 'did not find compelling evidence' that the subcoracoscapularis, the coracobrachialis, the latissimus dorsi, the triceps or the individual forearm muscles existed as SEPARATE muscles in early tetrapodomorph fish, though Andrews & Westoll (1970a) reconstructed all of them. The first individual correlate of this muscle appears one node crownward, at Elpistostegalia; under their alternative phylogeny, later still, at Acanthostega and crownward.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. A small mark on the posterior border of the scapulocoracoid, suggested by Andrews & Westoll (1970a) as a possible origin. Molnar et al. note that it is topologically consistent with the fossa or rugose area that carries the subcoracoscapularis in stem tetrapods, sitting beside the glenoid near the junction of the scapular and coracoid regions.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: Tiktaalik roseae. Molnar et al.'s character mapping puts the first individual osteological correlate of the subcoracoscapularis at this node — a triangular region on the scapulocoracoid dorsal and posterior to the glenoid — but what they report on the specimen itself, the MCZ cast of NUFV 112, is fainter: rugosities above the glenoid and a hollow above the coracoid foramen, 'well placed for the origins of deep dorsal musculature' and not assigned to a muscle. Under the Ahlberg et al. (2008) phylogeny the maximum-likelihood reconstruction delays the correlate to Acanthostega and crownward. Hence uncertain, and no attachment row.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. Origin from the posterior fossa on the scapulocoracoid dorsal to the glenoid (MGUH 1258, 1300); insertion on a process on the posterior edge of the humerus just proximal to the ectepicondyle, scarred on its ventral surface (Coates 1996), which Coates held homologous with 'process 2' of Ichthyostega. Where both a recess and a process are present, as in Crassigyrinus, Panchen (1985) read them as the insertions of separate subcoracoideus and subscapularis muscles — the division this record holds as one homology group.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. Scarring over the entire posterior face of the scapulocoracoid above the glenoid and much of its internal aspect, read by Bishop (2014) as the origin of the subcoracoscapularis ('subscapularis'). The same posterior fossa or triangular region is identified in Tulerpeton, Archeria, captorhinids and Pederpes, and as the 'supraglenoid fossa' of Eryops. Molnar et al. rate the reconstruction fairly confident once the character mapping is combined with the scars.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: Reported in urodeles by Smith (1926), Romer (1944) and Kardong (2002), but Abdala & Diogo flag the identification as needing confirmation.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: = subscapularis sensu Ecker (1889).

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: = subscapularis + subcoracoideus sensu Holmes (1977) and Dilkes (2000).

occurrences.name: Subscapularis
occurrences.origin: Subscapular fossa (medial surface of the scapula).
occurrences.action: Medially rotates the humerus; anterior stabiliser of the shoulder (rotator cuff).
occurrences.note: The coracoid contribution is lost with the coracoid itself; only the scapular head persists in therians.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The coracoid head is gone with the coracoid itself; only the scapular head persists, which is why the mammalian muscle is 'subscapularis' rather than 'subcoraco-scapularis'.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eudyptes pachyrhynchus, Schreiweis's type species. Both heads of this field. The subscapularis caput mediale arises from the proximal third of the costal scapula, a small area of the scapular process of the clavicle and the medial coracoid; the subcoracoideus from the dorsal spina externa of the sternum and the adjacent corpus sterni, further attaching to the dorsomedial coracoid. The two **fuse near the shoulder joint and insert by a common tendon**, which is why one record carries them. A wing-propelled diver: the flipper is the most derived forelimb in Aves, and these rows are an observation of a penguin, not of birds. That is exactly what species-level scoring is for — the old model refused this source rather than let it stand for the clade.

homology.notes: Consistent across Tetrapoda. The 'subcoraco-' prefix records the coracoid head present wherever a coracoid persists; its loss in therians is a consequence of girdle reduction, not of muscle loss.

muscles.name: Teres major
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass. Frequently differentiates in association with the latissimus dorsi.

consensus.origin: Posterior (caudal) border and inferior angle of the scapula.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus, adjacent to or shared with the latissimus dorsi insertion.
consensus.action: Retracts, adducts and medially rotates the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Lower subscapular / thoracodorsal nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.note: Marked '– [but see text]' by Abdala & Diogo.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin fleshy on the distolateral scapula; a long well-defined tendon to a bony ridge on the proximolateral humerus — a scar worth looking for in fossil pseudosuchians.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.origin: Inferior angle and lower lateral border of the scapula.
occurrences.insertion: Crest of the lesser tubercle of the humerus, with the latissimus dorsi.
occurrences.action: Adducts, extends and medially rotates the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From the aponeurosis covering subscapularis and immediately ventral to the caudal angle of the scapula, by a wide thin tendinous fascia onto the proximal medial humeral diaphysis.

homology.notes: Distribution is scattered — present in turtles, crocodylians and mammals, absent in amphibians and birds, uncertain in lepidosaurs. This pattern is more easily read as repeated differentiation from the latissimus dorsi/subcoracoscapularis field than as a single ancestral muscle with three losses.
homology.openQuestion: Is the turtle/crocodylian teres major homologous with the mammalian one, or convergent?

consensus.origin: Thoracolumbar fascia and the neural spines of the posterior thoracic and lumbar vertebrae; in non-mammalian tetrapods, the dorsal fascia over the anterior trunk.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus, on or near the crest of the lesser tubercle / deltopectoral region.
consensus.action: Retracts (extends) and adducts the humerus; the principal recovery-stroke muscle in sprawling locomotion.
consensus.innervation: Thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8) — dorsal (extensor) division of the brachial plexus.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.note: Scored uncertain, which corrects an earlier note here that claimed a dorsal humeral scar as its insertion. Molnar et al. report no compelling evidence that the latissimus dorsi existed as a muscle separate from the deltoideus in early tetrapodomorph fish; what marks the separation is the appearance of the latissimus dorsi process one node crownward.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. The only correlate is a shared one: the thickened posterior margin of the cleithrum above the glenoid, which Andrews & Westoll (1970a) read as the deltoideus plus part of the latissimus dorsi. There is no humeral correlate — the latissimus dorsi process is absent in this taxon and in Gogonasus, and first appears at Elpistostegalia.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tiktaalik roseae. The latissimus dorsi attachment is present as a process or a series of diagonal ridges (Vorobyeva 2000; Boisvert 2009; Ahlberg 2011), and its appearance at this node is what Molnar et al. read as the separation of the latissimus dorsi from the deltoideus. It sits at the proximal border of the ectepicondyle, which is why they take the muscle to be a derivative of the same superficial dorsal mass rather than a new arrival. In Strepsodus, Rhizodus and Aztecia the reported processes do not resemble these oblique ridges, and Molnar et al. score the latissimus insertion in those taxa as on the dorsal ridge itself.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. One or more ridges on the proximal dorsal humerus (Coates 1996), as in Tiktaalik and Panderichthys rather than the distinct spike of Baphetes and Pederpes; in Ichthyostega the process is probably confluent with the ectepicondyle. No origin is scored — the cleithral scar that would carry it cannot be separated from the deltoideus origin.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.note: Ossinodus pueri. Among the muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct 'fairly confidently' here by combining their character mapping with Bishop's (2014) scars, but they do not itemise which scar carries it, so no attachment row is scored.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.origin: Dorsal fascia.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior surface of the crista ventralis of the humerus, by a strong tendon.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The largest dorsal shoulder muscle, but its origin is entirely fascial — no bony attachment, so no correlate. The insertion is on the posterior face of the same crest that receives the pectoralis and supracoracoideus.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.note: Retained despite the carapace; origin shifts onto the internal surface of the shell.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin transferred onto the internal surface of the carapace, which is built from the ribs.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.origin: Dorsal fascia over the anterior trunk.
occurrences.innervation: Thoracodorsal equivalent from the dorsal divisions of the brachial plexus.
occurrences.note: In Varanus komodoensis the muscle is large and its humeral insertion is confluent with that of the teres complex (Kępa et al. 2023).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From an aponeurosis beside the dorsal midline — no bony origin — tendinously onto the proximal dorsal humerus. In Gekko the insertion shifts to the lateral side of the humerus, which is an attachment difference between two geckos and a caution against reading one lizard as Lepidosauria.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Alligator and Crocodylus, from Meers's descriptions. From the thoracodorsal fascia, beginning near the spinous process of the first dorsal vertebra and running linearly back to about the sixth dorsal rib; a large flat tendon passes between triceps longus lateralis and scapulohumeralis brevis to insert on the craniodorsal humerus in common with teres major. **The insertion leaves a large scar about a quarter of the shaft length from the humeral head, as a tubercle or a pit, and it is present even in hatchlings** — an osteological correlate reliable enough to use on a fossil.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pars cranialis is the most superficial back muscle, arising aponeurotically over the neural spines of three thoracic vertebrae rather than directly from bone, and inserting on the medial margins of the dorsal clavicle and the scapula.
occurrences.note: Schreiweis (1982) resolves the penguin muscle into cranialis, caudalis and metapatagialis parts.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.origin: Thoracolumbar fascia, spinous processes T7–L5, iliac crest, lower ribs.
occurrences.insertion: Floor of the intertubercular groove of the humerus.
occurrences.action: Extends, adducts and medially rotates the humerus.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.origin: Dorsal fascia over the anterior trunk.
occurrences.innervation: Thoracodorsal equivalent from the dorsal divisions of the brachial plexus.
occurrences.note: In Varanus komodoensis the muscle is large and its humeral insertion is confluent with that of the teres complex (Kępa et al. 2023).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. **Insertion shifted to the lateral surface of the humerus**, against the proximal dorsal surface in Eublepharis. Same bone, different face, and the shift diff reads it as a substantive move on the medial/lateral axis.

homology.notes: Unbroken across every taxon sampled and one of the few muscles whose insertion is reliably identifiable on fossil humeri. Its dorsal-mass derivation and thoracodorsal innervation are constant.
homology.teaching: Best single muscle for demonstrating that a large axio-appendicular muscle can survive a radical girdle rebuild (turtle shell, bird flight apparatus) without losing identity.

consensus.origin: Scapula near the glenoid (scapular head) plus one or more humeral heads along the shaft.
consensus.insertion: Olecranon process of the ulna.
consensus.action: Extends the elbow; the scapular head also retracts the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Radial nerve (C6–T1) — the defining nerve of the dorsal/extensor mass.

occurrences.name: Triceps
occurrences.note: Eusthenopteron foordi. Scored uncertain, and the earlier note here — 'inferred from the olecranon and from humeral shaft rugosities' — is wrong on this source's own evidence. Tetrapodomorph-fish ulnae lack an ossified olecranon; the olecranon and the posterior ulnar crest appear together at the last common ancestor of Tetrapoda, and their appearance is what Molnar et al. read as the separation of the triceps from the extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris. Here the superficial dorsal musculature probably inserted on the proximal ulna without leaving a mark (Andrews & Westoll 1970a). Molnar et al. call it tempting to homologise the dorsal process of the Latimeria ulna with the olecranon, and decline.

occurrences.name: Triceps
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. An ossified olecranon process with a confluent posterior crest, present in every stem tetrapod here whose ulna is preserved — Ichthyostega, where it is bifurcated and extremely well developed, Tulerpeton and Pederpes as well. Crassigyrinus is the exception: its presumed ulna appears to have neither feature. No origin is scored; the triceps leaves no correlate on the girdle in Iguana, and none is traced here.

occurrences.name: Triceps
occurrences.note: Ossinodus pueri. Among the muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct 'fairly confidently' here by combining their character mapping with Bishop's (2014) scars, but they do not itemise which scar carries it, so no attachment row is scored.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii (anconaeus group)
occurrences.note: Multi-headed in urodeles, with scapular and several humeral heads.
occurrences.origin: Four heads: coracoid (anconaeus coracoideus, by a long tendon); scapula posterior to the glenoid and the joint capsule (anconaeus scapularis medialis); proximal two-thirds of the lateral face of the humerus (anconaeus humeralis lateralis); the whole posterior face of the humerus (anconaeus humeralis medialis).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Four separately named heads, two girdle and two humeral, converging on one olecranon insertion. The coracoid and scapular heads unite about midway along the humerus. This is the clearest case in the dataset of a muscle whose head count is a naming decision: Mivart (1869) and Davison (1895) called the whole complex 'triceps', Francis (1934) named all four.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.action: In anurans, a major decelerator during landing rather than a propulsive extensor.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Insertion scars on the olecranon process.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Three heads: longus lateralis and longus medialis from the proximolateral scapula, brevis fleshy on the proximolateral humerus. All converge on the olecranon.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii (long, lateral, medial heads)
occurrences.origin: Infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula (long head); posterior humerus above and below the radial groove (lateral, medial heads).
occurrences.action: Extends the forearm; the long head also extends and adducts the arm.

homology.notes: Present in every tetrapod examined. The number of heads varies freely (three in mammals, more in urodeles and crocodylians) without disturbing the identity of the complex — a useful reminder that head count is not a homology criterion.
homology.teaching: The canonical dorsal-mass muscle: origin on the girdle and humerus, insertion on the ulna, radial innervation, elbow extension. Every other extensor can be introduced by reference to it.

muscles.name: Brachialis / humeroantebrachialis
synonyms: brachialis inferior (Romer 1944; Walker 1973; Holmes 1977; Dilkes 2000; Wyneken 2001)

consensus.origin: Anterior surface of the humeral shaft, distal to the deltopectoral crest.
consensus.insertion: Proximal ulna (and radius in some taxa).
consensus.action: Flexes the elbow. Because it crosses only the elbow, it is the pure elbow flexor regardless of forearm position.
consensus.innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6) — ventral division.

occurrences.name: Humeroantebrachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. The ventral median ridge of the radius, which usually carries obvious muscle scars and is read as the humeroantebrachialis insertion (Bishop 2014). Two statements in Molnar et al. sit awkwardly together: they list this ridge among the four longitudinal ridges of the radius in this taxon and label it in their Fig. 10F, yet their character mapping puts the ridge's first appearance at the last common ancestor of crown tetrapods, where it marks the separation of this muscle from the flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis. The row follows the description of the bone. No origin is scored — the ventromedial deltopectoral crest scars that carry it in Baphetes, Crassigyrinus and Ossinodus are not reported here.

occurrences.name: Humeroantebrachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. Origin from scars on the ventromedial aspect of the deltopectoral crest (Bishop 2014) — the same region Milner & Lindsay (1998) read as the humeroantebrachialis ('brachialis') origin in Baphetes and Smithson (1985) in Crassigyrinus; insertion on the ventral median ridge of the radius. In Necturus and Iguana the origin likewise includes part of the deltopectoral crest, which is the extant end of the same arrangement.

occurrences.name: Humeroantebrachialis
occurrences.note: In urodeles the brachialis field is not separated from the biceps field; the single muscle is called humeroantebrachialis.
occurrences.origin: Anterior surface of the proximal humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thick and parallel-fibred, crossing only the elbow. It has no girdle head, which is the difference from the amniote biceps brachii and the reason the two are not interchangeable.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the lateral and ventral humeral shaft to the proximal radius and ulna. In Gekko the origin is confined to the lateral shaft.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy on the anterior humeral head; inserts on the proximomedial radius with the biceps tendon.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.origin: Anterior surface of the distal half of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna.
occurrences.action: Flexes the elbow.
occurrences.innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6), with a variable radial contribution.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From a wide area of the lateral surface and craniodistal humeral diaphysis onto the medial ulna and the radius.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Origin **confined to the lateral humeral shaft**; in Eublepharis it takes the ventral surface as well.

homology.notes: The amphibian humeroantebrachialis and the amniote brachialis occupy the same field. Note the naming hazard: 'humeroantebrachialis' is used by Diogo & Abdala (2007) for the lepidosaur BICEPS, not the brachialis. Always check which sense an author intends.
homology.teaching: A terminology trap worth setting deliberately: the same name denotes different muscles in the urodele and lepidosaur literature.

muscles.name: Biceps brachii / coracoradialis
synonyms: short and long heads of biceps brachii (Jouffroy 1971)

consensus.origin: Coracoid or scapula near the glenoid — the muscle spans the shoulder as well as the elbow.
consensus.insertion: Radius (radial tuberosity), and via the bicipital aponeurosis to the antebrachial fascia in mammals.
consensus.action: Flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm; weak shoulder flexion.
consensus.innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6) — ventral division.

occurrences.note: Absent in Ambystoma ordinarium, but a coracoradialis is present in other urodeles.

occurrences.name: Coracoradialis
occurrences.note: The anuran name records the coracoid origin and radial insertion directly.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.note: = humeroantebrachialis sensu Diogo & Abdala (2007) and Diogo (2007); = short and long heads of biceps brachii sensu Jouffroy (1971).

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.note: Inferred from the biceps tubercle — an anteroposterior ridge on the lateroventral coracoid, named by Walker (1972) and treated as homologous across early crocodylomorphs by Crush (1980). Level I inference: the coracoid origin is bracketed by both Crocodylia and Aves.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: A discrete insertion tubercle on the radius.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: A very long tendon of origin from the ventral coracoid — about half the length of the belly — to the proximomedial radius.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii (long and short heads)
occurrences.origin: Supraglenoid tubercle (long head) and coracoid process (short head) of the scapula.
occurrences.action: Supinates the forearm and flexes the elbow.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The short head arises from the coracoid process — the fused remnant of the coracoid — rather than from a coracoid bone.

homology.notes: The coracoradialis/biceps field is continuous across Tetrapoda, distinguished from the brachialis by crossing the shoulder and inserting on the radius. Both are musculocutaneous-innervated, confirming shared ventral-mass derivation.

muscles.name: Coracobrachialis
synonyms: coracobrachialis superficialis/longus + profundus/brevis (Howell 1936a; Romer 1944; Jollie 1962; Holmes 1977; Dilkes 2000)

consensus.origin: Coracoid.
consensus.insertion: Medial or ventral surface of the humeral shaft.
consensus.action: Adducts and protracts (flexes) the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C7) — ventral division.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: Scored uncertain. Molnar et al. place the separation of the coracobrachialis from the pectoralis at the last common ancestor of Tetrapoda, marked by a distinct pectoralis process and coracobrachialis fossa on the humerus, and report no compelling evidence that it was a separate muscle in early tetrapodomorph fish.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. Two small pits on the ventral scapulocoracoid between the anterior and posterior buttresses read as the origin, and a large, shallow recess on the proximal ventral humerus as the insertion (Andrews & Westoll 1970a). The humeral recess is one of two correlates identified in this taxon and in no other tetrapodomorph fish, which Molnar et al. flag as reason for caution; Gogonasus has a comparable knob-like process on the ventral side between the buttresses.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. The rough, concave posterior region of the divided proximal ventral surface of the humerus (Coates 1996); the smooth anterior region beside it carries the supracoracoideus. Scored as humerus/ventral without a landmark — see the supracoracoideus row for why the anterior-posterior division between the two is in the note rather than in a second row.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: Ossinodus pueri. Among the muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct 'fairly confidently' here by combining their character mapping with Bishop's (2014) scars, but they do not itemise which scar carries it, so no attachment row is scored.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: Corresponds to the coracobrachialis longus/superficialis of Walthall & Ashley-Ross (2006).
occurrences.origin: Posterolateral surface of the coracoid.
occurrences.insertion: Medial face of the distal end of the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Its fibres run along the axis of the humerus to a distal insertion, so it retracts rather than adducts. Walthall & Ashley-Ross call it coracobrachialis longus; Abdala & Diogo record longus and superficialis as the same muscle.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: = coracobrachialis magnus + coracobrachialis brevis sensu Walker (1973) and Wyneken (2001).

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: = coracobrachialis superficialis/longus + coracobrachialis profundus/brevis of earlier authors.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: Inferred from a circular depression near the posterior margin of the lateroventral coracoid, shared with Dromicosuchus (NCSM 13733) and Terrestrisuchus. Crush (1980) read it as the attachment of the coracobrachialis anterior. Recorded here as an ORIGIN, which is this dataset's convention for the coracoid end; Crush and Bodenham et al. both word it as an insertion.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: = coracobrachialis brevis sensu Holmes (1977) and Dilkes (2000).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Klinkhamer et al. divide this into brevis ventralis and brevis dorsalis. The ventralis is scored here — fleshy over the entire lateral coracoid to the deltopectoral crest. They give the dorsalis an anterolateral SCAPULAR origin, which is not a coracoid attachment and is not folded in.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: = coracobrachialis longus + brevis, or cranialis + caudalis, or anterior + posterior, depending on author.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Coracobrachialis caudalis: one of two deep tongue-like muscles from the sternum, arising from the craniolateral corner of the sternal plane and the ventrolateral coracoid base, inserting on a shallow notch on the tuberculum ventrale of the proximal humerus.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.origin: Coracoid process of the scapula.
occurrences.insertion: Medial surface of the mid-humeral shaft.
occurrences.action: Flexes and adducts the arm.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin transfers to the coracoid process as the coracoid bone is lost.

homology.notes: Universal across Tetrapoda. Subdivision into two or three parts is frequent and independent; the number of parts carries no phylogenetic signal on its own. This muscle has the longest synonym list in the pectoral table — six naming schemes for the same field.
homology.teaching: Best illustration of why Abdala & Diogo's tables exist: the same muscle appears under six naming schemes across the literature.

consensus.origin: Proximal humerus.
consensus.insertion: Radius.
consensus.action: Flexes the elbow; in birds, tenses the propatagium — the leading-edge membrane of the wing.
consensus.innervation: Radial nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.note: Marked '– [but see text]'.

occurrences.name: Humeroradialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: A discrete insertion tubercle on the radius, separate from the biceps one.

occurrences.name: Humeroradialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy from the deltopectoral crest, inserting with biceps and brachialis.

occurrences.name: Humeroradialis / tensor propatagialis
occurrences.action: Tenses the propatagium, controlling the leading-edge camber of the wing.
occurrences.note: A striking case of exaptation: an archosaur elbow flexor recruited into the flight apparatus.

homology.notes: An archosaur muscle on this sampling. The bird tensor propatagialis is the same muscle as the crocodylian humeroradialis; the many bird-specific names obscure a straightforward homology.
homology.teaching: The propatagial tensor is a genuinely good exaptation example, and one that students can see in any bird wing.
